title: Why Plane Windows Have No Corners #science #engineering
description:
Look at any airliner window: the corners are always rounded. In 1954 the de Havilland Comet, the world's first jet airliner, broke up in midair twice. Every flight, the cabin is pressurised and then let down again, so the metal skin stretches and relaxes once per flight. Around a hole with a sharp corner, that stretch piles up in one small spot (a stress concentration). Over many flights a fatigue crack grew from the corner of a square cutout in the roof until the cabin burst; in a water-tank test a Comet fuselage burst the same way after about 3,000 pressure cycles (real and simulated flights). Rounded corners let the stress flow around the opening and spread out, which is why airliner windows have been rounded ever since.

More: Why does metal feel colder than wood? (long) https://youtu.be/peHjE4l3oDg

Sources
- FAA Lessons Learned: de Havilland DH-106 Comet 1, G-ALYP and G-ALYV accidents (fatigue of the pressure cabin; first fracture at the ADF window cutout)
- Report of the Court of Inquiry into the Comet accidents (1955)
- Engineering failure case studies: stress concentration at square window corners
- The pictures are schematic and not to scale; the stress lines show where the load crowds, not measured values

Every claim is checked against the sources above.
